items.desc: Research teams from INRAE, the University of Clermont Auvergne and the CNRS have reconstructed 10 ancient genomes (paleogenomes) that are the common ancestors of 84 botanical species of agronomic interest. Their work makes it possible to identify particular genes, shared across different species of plants and retained throughout their evolutionary history, that might play a key role in adapting to environmental constraints such as drought.

items.title: New measure captures how scientists' identities shift across academic disciplines
items.desc: Does the academic discipline of a scientist's doctorate accurately capture their disciplinary affiliation decades later? Consider a scientist who earned a doctorate in physics 25 years ago who now studies climate change, publishes primarily in interdisciplinary journals and considers herself a climate scientist. Does "physics" still accurately describe where she fits in science?

items.title: When will your glacier disappear? New website lets users explore risks worldwide
items.desc: When will the glacier in your valley disappear? Will the glacier you visited as a child still exist in 2050? And how much difference would limiting global warming make?

items.title: Bite, buzz, release: How bees make flowers give up their pollen
items.desc: Life is not always easy for a bee: Not all plants place their pollen outside. Some flowers have to be set to vibrating before the pollen can get out of their tube-like stamens. Certain bee species have developed a special technique for this: They bite on the flower and use their flight muscles to generate rapid vibrations. The stamen is shaken and the pollen is released. This phenomenon is known as "buzz pollination."

items.title: Unusual bonds reorganize structure and magnetism in vanadium material
items.desc: While chemical bonds usually determine the structure and properties of a material, bonds between neighboring metal atoms can also change as temperature or other conditions change. These changes can lead to unusual electronic and magnetic behaviors.

items.title: Shapeshifting plant roots rely on a balance of anatomy, metabolism, and microbes to maximize survival
items.desc: Scientists have identified the mechanisms that allow plants to change their root anatomy to maximize survival when nutrients are scarce. The findings could pave the way for developing new ways to improve beneficial plant-microbe interactions in agriculture.

items.title: Scientists discover a strange new form of ice that could help explain the interiors of Neptune and Uranus
items.desc: Scientists have discovered that there is ice deep inside planets like Neptune and Uranus and want to find out what form it takes and how it behaves. They cannot dig for it and transport it all the way back to Earth, so they do the next best thing: recreate those extreme conditions in the lab.

items.title: Smart pen detects pressure and movement to identify children's writing difficulties sooner
items.desc: A study by Politecnico di Milano and the University of Insubria (Varese and Como) has been published in PLOS Digital Health. The study involved more than 700 children from primary and lower secondary school. The participants used the THInkPen (Tele-Health Ink Pen) while completing two BVSCO-3 tasks from the Battery for the Clinical Assessment of Writing and Orthographic Skills. This is the most widely used test in Italy for assessing writing difficulties, dysgraphia and dysorthography.

items.title: Fertilizers and extreme heat are damaging coral reefs in the Gulf of Mexico, isotope analyses reveal
items.desc: Who isn't familiar with the colorful coral reefs from movies like "Finding Nemo" or "The Little Mermaid"? Unfortunately, the reality is often quite different, as these vital ecosystems are under pressure worldwide. Climate change and pollution are causing corals to bleach and die. Even the most resilient coral reefs of the United States are now threatened.

items.title: Giant volcanic blanket reveals hidden 'Pompeii' of Andean landscapes
items.desc: A vast sheet of volcanic rock in the Andes has preserved clues to a buried landscape that existed 22 million years ago, according to a new study led by UCL (University College London) researchers.

items.title: New study offers a detailed look at how wildfire smoke impacts Reno's air quality
items.desc: With Western wildfires increasing in size, duration and intensity, millions of Americans are now exposed to wildfire smoke each year. In California, 2020 and 2021 were particularly challenging, with a 10-fold increase in fires compared with any time in the state's history. Northern Nevada is positioned to receive much of the smoke from California wildfires, and Reno residents experienced months of smoke-shrouded skies during this time. Now, a new study gives us a deeper look into the potentially hazardous chemicals lurking in this smoke.

items.title: AI extracts interpretable constitutive laws directly from solid-mechanics data
items.desc: Researchers at the Eastern Institute of Technology (EIT), Ningbo, have developed a graph-based approach that directly extracts concise, accurate constitutive equations from solid-material experimental data. The study, published in Science Advances, describes a method for discovering constitutive models for alloy steels, lithium metal and filled rubbers. It outperforms mainstream empirical models in predictive accuracy while preserving explicit, physically interpretable mathematical formulations.

items.title: Healthy checkout policy shows promise for reducing soda sales and increasing healthy snack purchases
items.desc: In March 2021, Berkeley, Calif., became the first city in the world to ban the display of sugary beverages and snacks in store checkout lanes, where candy, chocolate and soda are commonly placed to encourage impulse buying while shoppers are in line.

items.title: Project RattleCam reveals baby snakes during birthing season in three US states for the first time
items.desc: It's the season for babies in the snake world, and Project RattleCam is capturing magical moments.

items.title: Brain's ability to hear a musical beat remains distinctly human, study suggests
items.desc: The seemingly trivial ability to hear a regular pulse in music is a remarkable—and perhaps distinctively human—feature of the brain. In a wide-ranging critical review, Gábor Háden of the HUN-REN Research Centre for Natural Sciences and Henkjan Honing of the University of Amsterdam evaluate more than two decades of research into how this capacity develops and has evolved. Their paper was published this week in the Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences.

items.title: Wasps are disappearing this summer, and scientists are worried
items.desc: Britain’s wasps have become mysteriously scarce this summer, and scientists suspect an unusual combination of temperature swings, heatwaves, and food shortages may be responsible. Even the wasps that remain appear unusually small, potentially offering a glimpse of how extreme heat could reshape insect populations.

items.title: Physicists just found a tiny glitch in time itself
items.desc: Unconventional quantum theories may imply that time itself has a tiny fundamental uncertainty, placing an ultimate limit on how precisely any clock could measure it. The effect is far beyond current detection, but it could reveal a hidden connection between quantum mechanics, gravity, and spacetime.

items.title: UNESCO warns there’s close to a 100% chance of a Mediterranean tsunami
items.desc: The Mediterranean may seem far removed from the world’s major tsunami zones, but history and modern modeling show that destructive waves can strike the French Riviera with surprisingly little warning. Some tsunamis could reach shore in under 10 minutes, while past events have produced waves around two meters high, powerful currents, damage, and deaths.

items.title: Scientists discover the human heart can regrow muscle after a heart attack
items.desc: Researchers have shown for the first time that human heart muscle cells can regrow after a heart attack. The finding overturns the idea that damaged areas of the heart are completely incapable of regeneration. Scientists now hope to identify ways to dramatically boost this natural repair process, potentially opening a new path toward treatments for heart failure.

items.title: Archaeologists find a 3,000-year-old Egyptian tomb before it’s too late
items.desc: While clearing debris to protect ancient Egyptian tombs from flash floods, researchers near Luxor stumbled upon an unknown 3,000-year-old tomb. Its remarkably preserved paintings depict an official named Paser, his wife, religious scenes, and offerings of food and flowers. The discovery comes as climate-driven flooding poses a growing threat to these fragile remains.

items.title: DNA solves the mystery of a body found in the Arctic in 1859
items.desc: Scientists have used DNA from living descendants to identify four more members of the doomed Franklin expedition, including Harry Peglar, whose identity had remained uncertain for 166 years. The findings offer new clues about the sailors who survived for years in the Arctic before joining the expedition’s ultimately fatal escape attempt.

items.title: The Moon may have formed intact just hours after a giant collision
items.desc: Scientists have discovered that the Moon-forming collision may have depended heavily on how hot and physically strong early Earth and Theia were. New simulations found that some impacts create the familiar disk of debris that later becomes the Moon, while others can produce an intact Moon in only about five hours. The results challenge the long-standing assumption that the enormous collision could be modeled as if both worlds behaved mostly like fluids.

items.title: UCLA scientists turn cord blood into powerful cancer-fighting T cells
items.desc: UCLA researchers developed ready-made cancer-fighting T cells from cord blood stem cells that can attack solid tumors through two separate detection systems. In mice, a single dose controlled cancer and extended survival while avoiding a dangerous complication associated with donor-derived T-cell therapies.

items.title: Scientists capture two DNA strands zipping together for the first time
items.desc: Scientists have directly observed how two negatively charged DNA molecules can pair up despite normally repelling each other. Positively charged metal ions appear to bridge the gap, helping matching DNA helices align groove for groove like a molecular zipper. The discovery confirms a theory proposed two decades ago and could help researchers understand DNA interactions involved in cancer and other cellular processes.

items.title: Scientists create brilliant white material without a drop of white pigment
items.desc: Researchers have created a foam-based material that produces intense whiteness and water repellency without titanium dioxide pigments or PFAS chemicals. Inspired by natural structures in snow, clouds, flowers, and lotus leaves, the material uses tiny pores to scatter light while its rough surface repels water. The technology could offer a more sustainable way to make white, water-resistant everyday materials.

items.title: Ancient teeth reveal humans were getting high 25,000 years ago
items.desc: Ancient human remains from Sulawesi suggest people were habitually using the psychoactive betel nut as far back as 25,000 years ago. Researchers found both unusual tooth wear and traces of arecoline, the nut’s mind-altering compound, in the teeth of prehistoric hunter-gatherers. The practice may have started partly as pain relief for toothaches, but prolonged use severely damaged their teeth. The discovery could represent the earliest known evidence of habitual drug use anywhere in the world.

items.title: Scientists find a bone-building switch that could fight osteoporosis
items.desc: An experimental compound called AP503 significantly strengthened bones in mice by activating GPR133, a receptor that boosts bone formation while slowing bone loss. Because the same treatment has also been linked to stronger muscles, researchers see intriguing potential for combating age-related decline and osteoporosis.

items.title: Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS is bursting with methanol
items.desc: Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS contains exceptionally high levels of methanol, suggesting it formed under conditions very different from those that shaped most comets in our solar system. ALMA also revealed that tiny icy grains around the comet are releasing methanol like miniature comets, giving astronomers an unusually detailed look at an object from another star system.

items.title: Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
items.desc: Two major alien-life announcements in 2025 generated enormous excitement, but most astrobiologists remained unconvinced. Only 6.6% of surveyed experts thought possible biological molecules on K2-18b probably represented extraterrestrial life, while 15.1% said the same about intriguing mineral patterns in a Martian rock.

items.title: 400,000-year-old teeth reveal a hidden link in human evolution
items.desc: More than 400,000-year-old Homo erectus teeth from China may reveal a surprising link between this ancient human species, Denisovans, and some modern people. Scientists found protein mutations suggesting several East Asian Homo erectus populations belonged to the same evolutionary group, including one mutation previously associated with Denisovans. That variant may have passed from Homo erectus into Denisovans and eventually reached modern populations in Southeast Asia and Oceania.

items.title: AI Could Make Governments Slower
items.desc: Governments are increasingly turning to AI tools to process vast amounts of information and make public services more efficient. But because human attention is finite, making machines more capable could simply create new bottlenecks wherever oversight is necessary.

items.title: Why Do So Few Women Work in India?
items.desc: India’s female labor force participation rate has long lagged behind that of peer economies like Bangladesh, not because of social norms, but because of weak demand for labor. That is ultimately good news, because it is a problem that can be solved with common-sense regulatory reforms and public investment.

items.title: Global Development’s Missing Ingredient
items.desc: Facing a democracy deficit worldwide, millions of vulnerable people lack avenues through which they can collectively negotiate their interests. Faith-based institutions committed to human dignity and pluralism can play an instrumental role in building the infrastructure required for grassroots organizing at scale.

items.title: China’s External Surplus Makes a “Mandarin Accord” Inevitable
items.desc: As with the Plaza Accord in 1985, when the United States and its major trading partners agreed to coordinate policies to weaken the US dollar, an agreement to address global imbalances emanating from China has become increasingly necessary. Given China’s undervalued currency, the situation simply cannot be sustained indefinitely.

items.title: War and Climate
items.desc: The closure of the Strait of Hormuz showed how quickly a regional conflict can throw global energy markets into chaos. By pushing governments toward coal and biofuels, the war could accelerate deforestation and undermine climate negotiations, with environmental consequences that will linger long after the fighting ends.

items.title: 9/11’s Long Shadow
items.desc: As tragic as the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, were, it was America’s response that truly changed the world. While it is difficult to pinpoint precisely which developments over the last 25 years were caused or compounded by 9/11, it seems clear that the event led the United States to abandon the principles that, with the Cold War over, were supposed to shape a better future.

items.title: The False Politics of Western Declinism
items.desc: Political leaders on both sides of the Atlantic increasingly portray the West as being in decline, even as their societies grow richer. By conflating a loss of relative economic power with falling living standards, they give populists an opening to turn domestic grievances into nationalist resentment.

items.title: The Big Picture
What 9/11 Did to Us
items.desc: For Americans who are old enough to remember them, the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks raised fundamental questions: Who could have done this, and above all, why? We now know that the answers would reshape the country and its place in the world—and not for the better.

items.title: After the AI Bubble Bursts
items.desc: Just as debt markets fueled the global financial near-meltdown that followed the 2007–08 subprime-mortgage crisis, their exposure to AI will drive developments now. The problem is that we possess only very limited public information about those markets, and regulators are not making that information any easier to obtain.

items.title: Trump Is Stoking Territorial Revisionism
items.desc: Donald Trump’s refusal to respect international borders has already led Argentina and Morocco to revive territorial disputes and has effectively given Israel carte blanche to operate where it sees fit. But this might be just the beginning: if the US can claim land and resources on the basis of vague national-security claims, anyone can.

items.title: Have the Terrorists Won?
items.desc: The point of terrorism is not to cause suffering, but to provoke the target into doing something that hurts it even more. In the quarter-century since the 9/11 attacks, the US has done just that, leaving the world and itself worse off.

items.title: How 9/11 Fractured the Global Order
items.desc: The terrorist attack on the United States 25 years ago remains among the most consequential events of this century. By fundamentally altering the trajectories of the United States and Russia, as well as that of a rising China, al-Qaeda’s attack set in motion developments that would produce the geopolitical tumult we live in today.

items.title: China’s Permanent Manufacturing Revolution
items.desc: In developed economies, manufacturing employment will decline, regardless of industrial strategies pursued. China's competitiveness means that any expectation that manufacturing will absorb more than a trivial fraction of the large increases in the working-age population still occurring in India or Africa is a delusion.

items.title: Europe Needs Dual-Use Defense Spending
items.desc: Some EU countries, such as Poland, are using their expanded defense budgets to buy more foreign hardware. A better approach would be to foster a thriving innovation ecosystem which ensures that the technologies, institutions, and people that underpin a strong military benefit the civilian economy as well.
